E087.transcription:
E087 - Handwritten Miller family tradition account

Diplomatic transcription prepared 19 September 2026 from the five-page image-only PDF supplied as nellie_alt_miller.pdf. Original spelling, capitalization, and punctuation are retained as closely as practical. Line wrapping is normalized into paragraphs. Words supplied or uncertain are enclosed in square brackets. Struck-out wording is omitted when a clear replacement is present. The scan remains authoritative.

PDF PAGE 1 (unnumbered manuscript page)

John William Alexander Miller

The Miller family history begins with John Wm A. the son of Abraham Miller. John was born about 1825 in Washington D. C. Near 1849-50 he married Anna Elizabeth Blackstone, who was born in Devonshire England. She had lived in a place of the same name as that of her father. If true such a circumstance would ordinarily indicate she came of a more or less landed gentry.

So far the family story poses a mystery unsolvable. As searching has been done in all areas without success.

How or where did John meet a lady of her class and who was disowned for marrying him. It is interesting to speculate on the circumstances of the match. But to find the facts requires a great deal more research.

To John and Anna Elizabeth was born a son named -

John Thomas Miller

Note

Since the above was written I have learned John W. A. Miller was born in Germany. Which clears up the problem of his marriage to Anna Elizabeth Blackstone. We can assume they were married in England. And now the search goes to there.

PDF PAGE 2 (manuscript page 2)

Son George also stated John went to Baltimore and worked as an apprentice under John Wm. Bruce. Which would indicate some friendly connection between the Miller and Bruce families.

John Wm Bruce worked for the Baltimore and Ohio railroad in their shops, as did as many as four or five of his sons through the years. While John Thomas was learning blacksmithing he lived with the Bruces. But apparently he did not follow the Bruces to Piedmont W. Va. when John Bruce was transferred to superintend the big Baltimore and Ohio shop there. No one of the Bruce family ever mentioned John Miller.

But in 1872 he went to Westernport, just across the river from Piedmont W. Va., to marry Annah Bruce. The marriage license dated 13, September 1872 shows Johns age as twenty and his residence as Baltimore Md. and painter as his occupation. Anna is noted as W. Anna Bruce age seventeen. She never used her name Williamannah. Who could blame her? What a terrible name to give a little girl. I think just because she was the seventh daughter and daddy thought he would never have another son he could name William, then he did have one right after Anna. He should have been more patient.

But back to John T. We wonder if he did learn to be a blacksmith. For painter fits better with the story of his being a carriage painter. And that he also made calling cards. And we know how they were so beautifully done by hand, and would be of the same fine painstaking form of art.

Johns and Annahs family soon began to arrive, and grow.

PDF PAGE 3 (newspaper clipping)

Funeral To Be Held Wednesday For J. T. Miller

Funeral services will be held this afternoon at 2:30 from the chapel of the Baldwin Park Funeral Home for John Thomas Miller, 87, of 1425 E. Valley boulevard, El Monte, who passed away November 20.

Mr. Miller, who was born April 17, 1851, at Washington D. C., had been a resident of El Monte three years and of the state 12 years.

The deceased a widower, is survived by three sons, Asa Miller, 217 Bogart street, John R. Miller, 134 N. Center street, Baldwin Park, and George Miller of St. Louis; and two daughters, Mrs. Emma Prosser and Mrs. Lula Lutten, both of 1425 E. Valley, El Monte.

Burial will be in the Rose Hills cemetery.

PDF PAGE 4 (manuscript page 3)

You can follow that growth on the family record sheet. She was such a little thing to have so many children. We know she was a small and attractive young girl.

The family started out with Charles Asa, as you can see, who was born in Westernport Md. Also the sister who followed him, the next little girl [Erma?] born in Piedmont W. Va., and both died in their infancy.

What a terrible blow to the young parents. Emma and Oliver were, also born in W. Va., William in Minnesota, John in Joliet Ill. also George, and Lula in E. St. Louis Ill.

Life was not easy for the little mother Annah. For John was a rover from his early years. The first long trip was made to Cedar Rapids Iowa when Oliver was only seven months old because he had a job there. They were a much traveled family before they finally landed in E. St. Louis. Johns itchy feet had kept them moving ever farther west. No wonder Charles Asa said the main thing he remembered was "moving."

The families life seemed settled down in St Louis. And the family grew up and some were married and had children. Son Olivers daughter told me the only thing she remembers about the family in St Louis was that her grandparents lived on a farm. That was just surprising! Nomads dont farm, they just move on to greener pastures. They really needed time to rest I guess.

But farm they did, or at least lived on one. For the grand daughter recalls all of the apples she ate there. And they must have raised a lot of carrots for I recall dad Asa saying he never wanted to eat another carrot, he got sick of them.

While the Millers lived in St. Louis many members of Annahs

PDF PAGE 5 (manuscript page 4)

Bruce family came to visit them, as many of them had passes for railroad travel and others were financially able to afford it, many made trips out to see them. This of course would have made Annah very happy. For she was so isolated from all of her fathers family.

It is not possible to say how long the family lived in St. Louis. But several of the family were married there and had there children born there. Son George was the only one of the family who never came west. He said the Bruces were still visiting in St Louis as late as 1905 as there were out to see the Worlds Fair there.

Some time along the way the family resided in Clifton, and there is no record of when they came to Calif. to live. Where six of them later died, correction, seven of the family died in California.

Not enough is known of Johns and Annahs family to give more than a few biographical notes.

Charles Asa was a plumbing and heating contractor. Olivers daughter said her father was a coal and ice dealer. He had the largest family, eight children. Asa had seven, but raised five. George had three, he was a city man, urbane, pleasant and self-assured. John was an inventor, a builder and full of ideas. He invented the home water heater. He served in World War I and fought in France. He and wife May had no children, neither did Erma, nor Wallace who married late and died very soon after. Lula had two children.

John and Annah did well as the progenitors and founders of the Miller clan and a family to be proud of who in turn have followed in their footsteps.

Note - John T. Miller came to Cal. in 1938

story.title: From Kentucky and Baltimore to California
story.introduction: A painter and public officer in nineteenth-century Baltimore. A son whose records carry the family west to California. A separately documented Kentucky Miller line whose Y-DNA connection may point toward their deeper paternal ancestry. Their lives emerge one document at a time—with some connections well supported and others still open.

events.title: An unsettled beginning
events.text: John William Alexander Miller's origins remain unresolved. His 1877 death certificate records Frederick County, Maryland, and an age of 52, pointing to a birth around 1824–1825. The man identified with him in the 1870 Baltimore census is 37 and Virginia-born. Both accounts remain part of the story.
events.caution: The age and birthplace disagree. No birth date or parentage is established by this comparison.

events.title: A Samuel Miller household in Pulaski County
events.text: A public surname index to the 1840 federal census lists a Samuel Miller household in Pulaski County, Kentucky. This agrees geographically with the later court petition's statement that Samuel's family came from Pulaski County.
events.caution: The original census image and household age tally have not yet been recovered. The index entry is supportive, but it does not alone prove this is the same Samuel or verify the reported 1837 arrival.

events.title: Samuel's move to Adair County and death
events.text: A sworn 1858 equity petition says Samuel Miller came from Pulaski County to a 150-acre tract on Russell Creek in Adair County in fall 1844. He died there about Christmas. His widow Huldah and the children remained temporarily, then returned to Pulaski County about 1847 or 1848.
events.caution: The petition establishes residence in Pulaski before fall 1844, but it does not establish Samuel's parents, Virginia origin, or the exact reported 1837 arrival year.

events.title: John Thomas's reported birth
events.text: John Thomas Miller's later death certificate gives his birth as 17 April 1851 in Washington, D.C. It names his father as John Miller and leaves his mother's maiden name unknown.
events.caution: This is a later death-record account, not a contemporary birth record. It does not name William Alexander, Abraham, or Blackstone.

events.title: A marriage in the District of Columbia
events.text: Three original register entries record the marriage of John W. A. Miller and Mary M. M. Lawson. The handwritten initial is W. Her possible identification with the later Margaret Miller is still a separate research question.
events.caution: The entries omit parents. They do not establish Abraham as John's father, and Mary and Margaret are not silently merged here.

events.title: Nine heirs name Samuel's Kentucky family
events.text: The Adair Circuit Court petition identifies James M., Jacob, John, Nancy, Walter, Henry, William F., Mary Jane, and Samuel C. Miller as Samuel's only children and heirs. Nancy's husband William Dugger joined the suit, and James M. acted for the four plaintiffs who were still under twenty-one.
events.caution: The petition calls Huldah Samuel's widow but does not expressly identify her as every heir's mother. The court case documents this Kentucky family; it does not prove how Samuel's paternal line connects to John W. A. Miller.

events.title: A painter on Raborg Street
events.text: Baltimore directories place John W. A. Miller in the painting trade: at 135 Raborg in 1864 and 129 Raborg in 1867. These addresses provide a thread of continuity through his later public-office records.

events.title: From the painting trade to public office
events.text: A Maryland legislative record names John W. A. Miller among Baltimore Ward 14 appointees. The 1868–69 directory lists him as a constable, with an office at 518 W. Baltimore and a dwelling at 129 Raborg. The 1870 directory again lists him as a constable on Raborg.

events.title: The family in Ward 14
events.text: The Baltimore household contains John W., a house painter, Margaret, and John T. The research identifies them with John William Alexander, Margaret Miller, and John Thomas Miller by correlating this household with later records and the wider Baltimore evidence.
events.caution: The census does not label family relationships. The father–son and spousal connections are research conclusions based on combined evidence.

events.title: John Thomas and Annah begin their married life
events.text: A marriage transcription records John T. Miller, a painter of Baltimore, marrying W. Anna Bruce of Piedmont. George W. Brooks of Westernport officiated. The license or record is dated 12 September, with the marriage on the following day.
events.caution: The transcription reports John as 22; that age differs from the birth date on his later death certificate.

events.title: A magistrate on West Baltimore Street
events.text: Directories continue the public-office trail: constable in 1872 and 1873, then magistrate in 1874 at 660 W. Baltimore Street.
events.caution: The 1872 address reading is provisional. An office address need not be a home address.

events.title: John W. A. Miller's death and burial
events.text: The death certificate records a married painter who died on 27 November 1877 and was buried at Western Cemetery on 29 November. The research identifies him with the Baltimore painter, constable, and magistrate. Burial references lead to plot 307-H.
events.caution: The certificate names no spouse, parents, or children. The identity conclusion retains the conflicting age and birthplace evidence.

events.title: Margaret and the shared cemetery plot
events.text: Margaret Miller's death certificate names her father as Lawson and her birthplace as Georgetown, D.C. Her memorial records Western Cemetery plot 307-H, the same plot associated with John W. A. Miller.
events.caution: The shared plot is strong association evidence. Neither document explicitly identifies her husband.

events.title: The next generation's household
events.text: The 1910 census describes John and Anna as married for 38 years, with nine children born and seven living. William and Lula appear in the household. The 1920 census again records John, Anna, William, and Lula, while the reported parental birthplaces continue to vary.

events.title: Their lives end in Alhambra
events.text: Annah died in Alhambra, California, on 7 September 1936. John Thomas died there on 20 November 1938. His death certificate describes a blacksmith who retired in 1913 after 30 years in the occupation. Their death records place their burials at Rose Hill / Rose Hills Memorial Park.

coverage.area: Abraham versus Leonard name and identity test, 18 September 2026
coverage.finding: Abraham/Abram and Leonard/Leonhard/Leonhardt are distinct given names, not German-English spelling equivalents. The 1830 same-page census establishes two separate household heads under those names, so Leonard was not simply enumerated as Abraham. No reviewed record calls Leonard Abraham, Abraham Leonard, Abram or otherwise supplies a double name. The next useful question is whether the two men were relatives or associates, tested through tax, deed, estate and church records.

coverage.area: Frederick probate indexes for Leonard Miller
coverage.finding: On 18 September 2026 the L-surname pages of the Frederick County will index and Estate Docket T91/C787-2 were reviewed without finding Leonard Miller as a decedent. The original 5 January 1836 bond now proves that Leonard was a surety for the administrators of Abraham Miller's estate. This establishes direct association but not brotherhood, guardianship or parentage. Index absence does not prove that Leonard left no estate or died outside Frederick County.

coverage.area: Frederick probate lead for Abraham Miller, 18 September 2026
coverage.finding: The original estate records supersede the earlier docket interpretation. A $2,000 administration bond dated 5 January 1836 names Susanna Miller and Jacob T. C. Miller as administrators of Abraham Miller, with Leonard Miller and George Main as additional obligors. January and March 1836 inventories repeat the administrators; the goods include an enslaved woman named Nancy and a child but name no heirs. The recovered account of sale says the property was sold 6 February 1836 and repeatedly names Jacob T. C. Miller as a purchaser, together with Susanna or Susan, Daniel, George or George W., and Elizabeth Miller and Mary Hedges. This concentrated purchaser group strongly supports a household or close-kin network but states no relationships. One purchaser is machine-read as 'Leo M. Miller'; the manuscript is too indistinct to identify him as Leonard, whose bond role remains the controlling association. The 1839 first and final account calls Abraham late of Frederick County and closes without a distribution to named heirs. This closely matches the derivative Abraham-Susanna family that names Jacob Thomas Creager Miller and makes the Frederick network the leading candidate, while the lack of a boy age 5-9 in Abraham's 1830 household and the absence of any named John keep parentage low confidence. Exact-name searches of the 1815-1844 Orphans Court proceeding indexes returned no Abraham/Leonard guardianship entry; tracing the sale purchasers and recovering loose estate papers are now highest priority.

coverage.area: Washington County Abraham candidate, 1820-1865, reviewed 18 September 2026
coverage.finding: An Abraham Miller headed a Washington County District 1 household in 1820 with a male age 26-44, female 16-25, boy under 10 and seven enslaved people. In 1830 a District 1 Abraham age 40-49 headed a ten-person free household with sons in four consecutive brackets, including one boy age 5-9 who exactly fits John if born about 1824-1825. The only indexed 1840 Abraham found was a different Clear Spring head age 20-29, but that gap is superseded as evidence of disappearance: in 1850 a Maryland-born Abraham age 62, farmer with $13,000 real estate, headed a Subdivision 2 household with Catharine 52 and eight younger people. The head ages and several household slots make 1830-to-1850 continuity plausible, not proved; the 1850 census states no relationships and contains no adult John. A Washington County probate index and newspaper notice place Abraham's estate in October 1865. The original 10 October bond in volume G, page 430 confirms Joseph Garver as estate representative and names Isaac Garver and Christian Newcomer as additional bondsmen. The original inventory in volume V, pages 373-376, records a $468.14 personal estate, names John L. Newcomer and probably George Fulton as appraisers, and was affirmed by Joseph Garver on 17 October. It names no relatives or specific residence. The estate is not yet proved to be the 1850 man; sale records, accounts and distribution remain the most direct route to named heirs. Four obvious age-compatible 1850 Washington County John candidates were also reviewed without producing a father Abraham. An earlier wife or child was not treated as disqualifying because of the Anna Elizabeth Blackstone tradition; the John W./Sarah candidate was excluded only after he was traced continuously with Sarah and their children through 1860 and 1870, overlapping the target's later family. This is a bounded negative. The major weakness remains geography: Washington County was separate from Frederick County at the target birth, so John's death-record birthplace would have to be wrong or regionally simplified.

coverage.area: Broader Abraham identity and generation review, 18 September 2026
coverage.finding: Derivative family pages report an Abraham Miller about 1765-1835 married to Susanna Creager and name Jacob Thomas Creager Miller as a son. Indexed Saint John Evangelical Lutheran records at Creagerstown now explicitly identify Abraham Miller and Susanna or Sussanna as parents of Johannes, born 25 August 1795 and christened 6 March 1796, and Anna Maria, born 17 December 1797 and christened 9 April 1798. The underlying images were unavailable. The Anna Maria record independently confirms a reported daughter and gives the Mary Hedges estate-sale purchaser a plausible identity that still needs marriage/later-life proof. Original 1836-1839 probate independently supplies the same uncommon Susanna and Jacob T. C. names as Abraham's administrators, and the sale repeatedly shows Jacob purchasing property alongside Susanna or Susan and a concentrated Miller/Hedges group. This raises the identity overlay to moderate confidence and makes Jacob's reported son relationship persuasive, but no reviewed original explicitly calls him a son. The earlier Johannes is a substantial caution against assigning the target John, born about 1824-1825, to this couple unless the earlier child died or another explanation is proved. A derivative 1802 Frederick list names constable Abraham Miller, junior, while an official 1778 muster names an earlier Abraham Miller, Jr.; these establish repeated local senior/junior naming, not a proved genealogy. A separately reconstructed Falling Waters/Berkeley County Abraham born 1791 had named spouses and eight reported children but no target John, making him increasingly disfavored.

coverage.area: 1825 Frederick County boundary coverage
coverage.finding: Carroll County was formed in 1837 from parts of Frederick and Baltimore counties. A birth described in 1877 as Frederick County in 1824-1825 may therefore fall in a church or later index filed under present-day Carroll County. MSA advises checking Frederick and Baltimore indexes for pre-1837 Carroll territory. This is a jurisdictional lead, not evidence that the target lived in eastern Frederick County.

coverage.area: Samuel Miller Kentucky timeline and heirs, 2026-09-20
coverage.finding: Visually reviewed the original equity-case cover and sworn petition at PDF pages 1-6 and preserved the complete 102-page scan. The petition names James M., Jacob, John, Nancy (wife of William Dugger), Walter, Henry, William F., Mary Jane and Samuel C. Miller as Samuel's only children and heirs; the last four were under twenty-one in January 1858. It identifies Huldah as Samuel's widow, not expressly as the children's mother. The family came from Pulaski County to Adair County in fall 1844, Samuel died there about Christmas, and the widow and children returned to Pulaski about 1847 or 1848. A derivative 1840 Pulaski census surname index contains Samuel Miller, but the original image and age-column tally are still needed. The exact 1837 arrival remains a reported claim rather than an original-record conclusion.
